name: SQL
year_note: Chamberlin and Boyce began work on SEQUEL at IBM San Jose in 1973 (Wikipedia's infobox gives 1973) and published it in May 1974. It was renamed SQL for trademark reasons; commercial implementations appeared from 1979, and ANSI and ISO standardized it in 1986–87.
tagline: The declarative language of relational databases: describe the rows you want and let the engine work out how to get them.
summary: SQL is a declarative, domain-specific language for defining, querying and updating data in relational database management systems. Designed at IBM as SEQUEL for the System R prototype, it expresses Edgar F. Codd's relational model in English-like keywords: a query describes the result, and a query optimizer chooses how to compute it. Standardized by ANSI and ISO since 1986, it remains the dominant database language, spoken in vendor dialects by systems from SQLite to Oracle.
history:
In 1970 Edgar F. Codd of IBM published the relational model of data. His colleagues Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce first designed SQUARE, a query notation whose subscripts and superscripts proved hard to use; after moving to IBM's San Jose Research Laboratory in 1973 they began its sequel, SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language), described in a May 1974 paper; Boyce died that June, weeks after its publication. SEQUEL became the language of the System R research prototype, and was renamed SQL because 'SEQUEL' was a trademark of the British company Hawker Siddeley Dynamics Engineering.

Relational Software, Inc. (now Oracle) shipped one of the first commercial SQL systems, Oracle V2, in June 1979, while IBM's System R-derived products — System/38, SQL/DS and DB2 — appeared in 1979, 1981 and 1983; IBM's endorsement moved the industry to SQL from alternatives such as QUEL. ANSI standardized SQL in 1986 and ISO in 1987. SQL-92 was a major revision; SQL:1999 added recursive queries, triggers, procedural control flow and object-relational types; later editions added window functions (2003), JSON (2016) and property-graph queries (2023). Every major database implements its own dialect of the standard.
innovations: Made Codd's relational model practical as an English-like, non-procedural query language
Declarative queries whose execution plan is chosen by a query optimizer rather than the programmer
One language for data definition, manipulation and access control
Set-at-a-time processing with joins, grouping and aggregation
Recursive common table expressions (SQL:1999) for transitive closure and other recursive queries

typing.notes: Columns and expressions have SQL types that are checked when a statement is prepared, with three-valued logic for NULL. SQLite is a notable exception, using dynamic 'type affinity'.

influenced_by_external.name: Relational model (E. F. Codd)
influenced_by_external.note: 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks' — the theory SQL was designed to make usable.

influenced_by_external.name: SQUARE
influenced_by_external.note: Chamberlin and Boyce's earlier relational query notation; SEQUEL was conceived as its sequel.

influenced_by_external.name: Datalog
influenced_by_external.note: Listed by Wikipedia; its influence shows in SQL:1999's recursive queries rather than in the 1974 design.

declarative-queries.note: SELECT describes the result; the optimizer picks join order, indexes and algorithms.

static-typing.note: Declared column types; SQLite is dynamically typed.

recursion.note: Recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE); SQL/PSM routines can also recurse.

structured-control.note: IF, CASE, LOOP and WHILE in stored routines (ISO/IEC 9075-4); vendor dialects such as PL/SQL, T-SQL and PL/pgSQL predate or extend it.

exceptions.note: Condition handlers (DECLARE … HANDLER) and SIGNAL/RESIGNAL in stored routines.

regex-builtin.note: SIMILAR TO (SQL:1999) and LIKE_REGEX (SQL:2008) extend the original LIKE wildcards.

reflection.note: INFORMATION_SCHEMA views expose the schema as queryable tables, and DDL can change it at run time.

classes.note: Structured user-defined types with methods; rarely implemented (Db2 and Oracle object types).

inheritance.note: Type and table hierarchies with UNDER; rarely used in practice.

milestones.event: Codd publishes the relational model of data
Chamberlin and Boyce publish SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language
Relational Software ships Oracle V2, one of the first commercial SQL databases
IBM releases DB2, following System/38 (1979) and SQL/DS (1981)
ANSI standard SQL-86 (adopted by ISO in 1987)
SQL-92, a major revision of the standard
SQL:1999 adds recursive queries, triggers, procedural statements and structured types
SQL:2003 adds window functions and SQL/XML
SQL:2016 adds JSON operations and row pattern matching
SQL:2023 adds a JSON data type and property graph queries (SQL/PGQ)

trivia: SEQUEL was so named because it was the sequel to Chamberlin and Boyce's earlier language, SQUARE.
It was shortened to SQL because 'SEQUEL' was a trademark of the British company Hawker Siddeley Dynamics Engineering.
The standard prescribes the pronunciation 'ess-cue-el', but many practitioners — including Chamberlin — say 'sequel'.

hello.notes: SQL has no 'program': a query returns a table and the client prints its rows. SELECT without FROM is a near-universal extension; strict ISO SQL requires a FROM clause (or VALUES ('Hello, World!')).

factorial.code:
-- No recursive functions here: recursion lives in a
-- recursive common table expression that builds a relation (n, n!).
WITH RECURSIVE factorial(n, f) AS (
  SELECT 0, 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1, f * (n + 1) FROM factorial WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT f FROM factorial WHERE n = 10;
factorial.notes: Standard SQL queries cannot define recursive functions (SQL/PSM and vendor procedural dialects can); instead, a SQL:1999 recursive CTE builds the relation of (n, n!) pairs. SEQUEL (1974) had no recursion at all.

fizzbuzz.code:
WITH RECURSIVE nums(i) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT i + 1 FROM nums WHERE i < 15
)
SELECT CASE
         WHEN i % 15 = 0 THEN 'FizzBuzz'
         WHEN i % 3 = 0  THEN 'Fizz'
         WHEN i % 5 = 0  THEN 'Buzz'
         ELSE CAST(i AS VARCHAR(2))
       END AS fizzbuzz
FROM nums
ORDER BY i;
fizzbuzz.expected_output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
fizzbuzz.notes: % is the near-universal modulo operator; the standard spells it MOD(i, 15), but SQLite's mod() returns a floating-point value. ORDER BY is required — without it row order is unspecified — and the alias keeps PostgreSQL from sorting by the output column.

higher-order.code:
-- Filter with WHERE, map with the SELECT list, fold with an aggregate.
WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (
  SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 10
)
SELECT string_agg(CAST(n * n AS VARCHAR(3)), ' ' ORDER BY n)
FROM nums
WHERE n % 2 = 0;
higher-order.notes: WHERE filters, the SELECT list maps and an aggregate folds. string_agg with an in-aggregate ORDER BY works in PostgreSQL and SQLite ≥ 3.44; the ISO spelling is LISTAGG(…) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY n) (SQL:2016), and MySQL uses GROUP_CONCAT.

shapes.notes: Relational modelling: one table per kind of shape, and a view (UNION ALL) as the common 'area' interface. A single table with a kind column and CASE is the other common design. Integer division truncates.

signature.title: Say what, not how
signature.code:
-- Data lives in relations (tables); a query states WHAT to find,
-- and the engine's planner decides HOW (join order, indexes...).
CREATE TABLE language  (name VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, year INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE influence (parent VARCHAR(20), child VARCHAR(20));

INSERT INTO language VALUES
  ('Lisp', 1958), ('ML', 1973), ('Scheme', 1975),
  ('Miranda', 1985), ('Haskell', 1990), ('OCaml', 1996);
INSERT INTO influence VALUES
  ('Lisp', 'ML'), ('Lisp', 'Scheme'), ('ML', 'Miranda'), ('ML', 'Haskell'),
  ('ML', 'OCaml'), ('Miranda', 'Haskell'), ('Scheme', 'Haskell');

-- Which languages influenced at least two others, and when was the first?
SELECT p.name, COUNT(*) AS children, MIN(c.year) AS first_child
FROM language p
JOIN influence i ON i.parent = p.name
JOIN language c  ON c.name = i.child
GROUP BY p.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY children DESC, p.name;
signature.notes: Printed in the sqlite3 shell's default list mode (columns separated by |); psql -A -t prints the same. The explicit JOIN … ON syntax dates from SQL-92; earlier SQL listed the tables in FROM and put join conditions in WHERE.
